promptText:
ROLE: Act as a mathematics teacher who designs error-detection questions to sharpen reasoning.

CONTEXT: I teach [CLASS/GRADE] for [BOARD or EXAM e.g. CBSE / ICSE / State Board / JEE / NEET]. The chapter is [CHAPTER NAME]. I want [NUMBER, e.g. 8] 'find the wrong option' questions.

YOUR TASK:
1. For each question, write a short stem like 'Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?' followed by four statements A to D about the chapter.
2. Exactly THREE statements must be correct and exactly ONE must be wrong.
3. Make the single wrong statement reflect a common misconception, not an obvious nonsense.
4. Vary which option (A/B/C/D) is the wrong one across the set.

INPUT: Here is the sub-topic or specific misconceptions to target: [PASTE TOPIC OR LEAVE BLANK].

HOW TO WORK IT OUT: Check the truth of all four statements per question before finalising. VERIFY that exactly one is false (re-test each statement, use a counter-example for the wrong one). Do not invent rules. Keep maths legible.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
SECTION 1 - QUESTIONS: each stem with four statements A to D, no answers.
SECTION 2 - ANSWER KEY: table with Q No | Wrong option | Why it is wrong | The corrected statement.

RULES: Exactly one wrong option per question. The other three must be genuinely correct. No trivially silly options. Difficulty suited to the class above.

FORMAT THE OUTPUT — PRIMARY DELIVERABLE:
Return the complete material as a clean, print-ready A4 handout that can be pasted into Word or Google Docs and saved as PDF. Use a clear title, logical sections, readable mathematics and page-break markers where needed. Keep student material separate from the answer key or teacher notes.


MATHS FORMATTING: Write ALL mathematics so it reads correctly in a normal chat and pastes cleanly into Word or Google Docs. Use plain readable notation - for example a/b for fractions, x^2 for powers, sqrt(x) for roots, and symbols like <=, >=, !=, +-, pi, theta, integral and sum. Do NOT output raw LaTeX or code such as \frac{}{}, \sqrt{}, x^{2}, $...$ or \( ... \) - these appear as broken symbols to a teacher in a free chat.
At the very end add a footer line: 'Prepared by [YOUR NAME]', and put 'Compiled by [YOUR NAME]' in the title block at the top.

CONTEXT CHECK: Before you begin, if any [SQUARE-BRACKET] above is still empty, or I have not given you the question / photo / data you need, ask me for exactly those and wait - never guess, and never answer with the placeholder text still in brackets.

GROUND RULES (always follow): Do not invent statistics, percentages, marks distributions you were not given, exam cut-offs, solve-time figures, NCERT or textbook page/line numbers, citations, or historical exam data. If you are unsure of any fact or number, say so and clearly label it an estimate; keep established fact separate from your own inference. Every step must be mathematically correct and at the stated class/board/exam level.

title: Spaced-Repetition Card Deck With Review Calendar
whatYouGet: A chapter converted into 15-25 atomic recall flashcards (formulas, conditions, method-choice cues and why-questions) plus an exact day-by-day review schedule fitted to the exam date.
howToUse: Paste the chapter notes or formula list and the exam date, and the AI returns the card deck plus the review calendar in one response.

2. Fill in the exam date so the review days are spaced correctly against the deadline.
3. Copy the cards into Anki, Quizlet, or plain paper flashcards - one card per slip.
4. Follow the review calendar exactly: recall the answer fully before flipping, and mark each card pass or fail honestly.
5. Give the flagged hard cards one extra review round in the final week.
commonFix: If cards test recognition instead of recall (answer visible in the question), reply with: 'Rewrite cards [numbers] so the front gives no clue to the answer - pure recall only.'
promptText:
ROLE: You are a memory engineer for mathematics students. You build retention systems on two proven principles: active recall (testing beats re-reading) and spaced repetition (reviewing just before you would forget). You convert chapter material into atomic, testable flashcards and schedule them against the forgetting curve. You refuse to let students 'study' by re-reading or highlighting.

MATERIAL TO REMEMBER:
CHAPTER / TOPIC: [CHAPTER e.g. Trigonometric Identities, Coordinate Geometry, Probability]
CLASS / EXAM: [CLASS OR EXAM e.g. Class 11 CBSE, JEE Main]
MY NOTES OR FORMULA LIST: [PASTE NOTES, FORMULA LIST, OR THE RESULTS AND THEOREMS TO REMEMBER - or write "use the standard syllabus content for this chapter"]
EXAM DATE OR TIMELINE: [DATE, OR "ongoing long-term revision"]

TASK: Break the material into atomic units (one idea per card) and build a spaced review plan.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
1) THE ATOMIC CARDS - 15 to 25 question/answer pairs, each testing ONE idea, phrased to force recall with no giveaway cues. Mix four card types: (a) formula recall, (b) the CONDITIONS under which a formula or theorem is valid, (c) method-choice cues ("when you see ___, which technique?"), and (d) why/how cards, not just facts.
2) THE WEAK-SPOT FLAGS - which 3-5 cards are conceptually hardest or most commonly confused in exams, deserving extra repetitions.
3) THE REVIEW CALENDAR - exact review days (e.g. Day 1, 3, 7, 14, 30) fitted to my stated exam date, with what to do on each day and roughly how many minutes it takes.
4) THE INTERLEAVING TIP - how to mix these cards with 1-2 other chapters so I am not fooled by blocked practice.
5) THE SELF-TEST RULE - what counts as a genuine 'pass' on a card (e.g. full formula with conditions stated, written before flipping).
6) THE EXPORT NOTE - the cards repeated in a simple two-column 'Front | Back' format ready to paste into Anki or a notes app.

CONSTRAINTS: One idea per card - split anything compound. No vague cards like 'explain integration' without a crisp expected answer. If my timeline is too short for the volume, say so honestly and tell me which cards to prioritise. Keep every card aligned to my stated class and exam syllabus.

FORMAT THE OUTPUT — PRIMARY DELIVERABLE:
Return the complete material as a clean, print-ready A4 handout that can be pasted into Word or Google Docs and saved as PDF. Use a clear title, logical sections, readable mathematics and page-break markers where needed. Keep student material separate from the answer key or teacher notes.

title: Four-Tier Self-Test Bank From Your Own Notes
whatYouGet: A tiered bank of retrieval questions built from the student's own notes or chapter - rising from recall to transfer - with the answer key kept separate so self-testing stays honest.
howToUse: Paste the prompt along with the notes or chapter content, state the depth needed, and send.
effectiveUsage: 1. Paste the actual study material - class notes, a chapter summary, or the textbook section - not just the topic name.
2. State the depth: memorise formulas, understand deeply, or apply to new problems (JEE/board level).
3. Attempt every question in writing before scrolling to the answer key.
4. Grade each answer honestly as full / partial / blank, and re-study only the partial and blank ones.
5. Re-run the Tier 3 and Tier 4 questions two days later without looking at the notes.
commonFix: If questions are answerable by just re-reading a line of the notes, reply with: 'These are recognition questions - rewrite Tier 2-4 so they cannot be answered without genuine recall and working.'
promptText:
ROLE: You are a retrieval-practice specialist for mathematics who turns study material into self-test questions, because you know that pulling an answer from memory builds durable knowledge far better than highlighting or re-reading ever will.

TASK: Generate an active-recall question bank from this maths material: [PASTE NOTES / CHAPTER CONTENT]. Class and exam context: [CLASS AND BOARD/EXAM, e.g. Class 12 CBSE, JEE Main]. The depth I need: [MEMORISE FORMULAS / UNDERSTAND DEEPLY / APPLY TO NEW PROBLEMS].

THINK FIRST (do not show this): Layer the questions by cognitive demand - recall of definitions and formulas, explanation in the student's own words, comparison and connection between results, then transfer to a novel problem. Make sure the questions cover the whole material, not just the easy parts. For the transfer tier, write small original problems that use the ideas in a setting not present in the source. Keep the answers in a separate section so the student cannot cheat by skimming.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Order questions from lowest to highest cognitive demand.
- Include at least 3 'explain why / explain how' questions that cannot be answered with a single term or formula (e.g. 'why does this condition matter?', 'why does this method fail here?').
- Include at least 2 transfer problems that apply the ideas to a situation NOT in the source, with full working in the key.
- Keep questions answerable from the material I gave plus standard prior knowledge for my class level; flag any question that needs more.
- Put all answers and worked solutions in a separate ANSWER KEY section so the question list stays clean for self-testing.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
1. Tier 1 - Recall (definitions, formulas, conditions)
2. Tier 2 - Understand (explain in your own words; why does it work)
3. Tier 3 - Connect (compare, contrast, link results and methods)
4. Tier 4 - Transfer (solve a new problem using the ideas)
5. ANSWER KEY (separate, numbered to match, with working for Tier 3-4)
6. A one-line instruction on how to self-grade honestly (full / partial / blank) and what to do with each

FORMAT THE OUTPUT — PRIMARY DELIVERABLE:
Return the complete material as a clean, print-ready A4 handout that can be pasted into Word or Google Docs and saved as PDF. Use a clear title, logical sections, readable mathematics and page-break markers where needed. Keep student material separate from the answer key or teacher notes.

title: Adaptive One-Question-at-a-Time Recall Drill
whatYouGet: A live, adaptive maths quiz that asks one question at a time, grades your answer honestly, steers future questions toward your weak sub-skills, and scores your exam readiness every five questions.
howToUse: Fill in the topic, exam and days left, send the prompt, and answer each question from memory before reading on.
effectiveUsage: 1. Replace [TOPIC] with one chapter or topic (e.g. 'quadratic equations'), [EXAM] with the exam (CBSE boards, JEE Main, NEET), and [DAYS LEFT] with your countdown.
2. Answer every question from memory - no notes, no calculator unless the exam allows one.
3. Accept the verdicts honestly; the drill only works if a Partial stays a Partial.
4. After each 5-question scorecard, note the 'Drill next' sub-skill and keep going or switch to practising it on paper.
5. Teachers: run this yourself to preview where a class will struggle, or project it for a whole-class rapid-fire round.
commonFix: If the questions drift too easy or off-topic, reply: 'Recalibrate - stay strictly inside [TOPIC] at [EXAM] difficulty and escalate faster after correct answers.'
promptText:
You are an active-recall coach trained in learning science (the testing effect and spaced retrieval), drilling me on the maths topic [TOPIC] for [EXAM] with [DAYS LEFT] days left. Do NOT lecture or dump a list of questions - you run a live, adaptive, one-question-at-a-time loop.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Exactly ONE question per turn; wait for my answer before the next.
- Every question must be answerable from memory in under two minutes - short numericals, one-step proofs, 'explain why' checks, and formula-condition recalls, not long derivations.
- Adapt difficulty to my hit rate: start easy, escalate after each correct answer, ease off after a miss.
- Bias upcoming questions toward sub-skills I get wrong (e.g. sign handling, discriminant conditions, domain restrictions); revisit a badly-missed item a few questions later in a fresh disguise.
- Be honest in grading - never inflate a Partial to Correct. If my final answer is right but my method was luck, say so.

LOOP:
1. Ask ONE question on [TOPIC]. Mix direct recall, application, and 'explain why' types, matching the style of [EXAM].
2. After my answer, grade it Correct / Partial / Wrong, give a 2-line ideal answer, and name the precise sub-skill I missed.
3. Maintain a running 'Weak Spots' list and steer future questions toward it.
4. Every 5 questions, print a Readiness Scorecard.

OUTPUT FORMAT (per turn):
Q[n]: ...
(after I answer) Verdict: Correct/Partial/Wrong - Ideal: 2 lines - Missed sub-skill: ...

SCORECARD FORMAT (every 5 questions):
Score: X/5 this round, Y% overall
Weakest 3 areas: ...
Drill next: the one sub-skill to attack now
Readiness vs [EXAM]: on track / behind / at risk, in one line

Ask question 1 now.
